subject: Cognitive Science
title: Mental Models Theory
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mental Models Theory.

hook.text: You don't use formal logic in your head. You build tiny mental scenarios and check if conclusions hold.

buildup.text: Johnson-Laird's mental models theory: we reason by building and inspecting mental representations.

discovery.text: We construct one model, check it, and conclude. Errors arise when we fail to build alternative models.

twist.text: Problems requiring multiple models are exponentially harder. Working memory limits how many we can hold.

climax.text: This explains why logical errors are predictable: they occur exactly where multiple models are needed.

punchline.text: We reason with models, not rules. And models have limits.

quiz.question: What does mental models theory claim about reasoning?
options: We reason by building mental representations, not formal rules

details.summary: Philip Johnson-Laird's mental models theory proposes that people reason by constructing and manipulating mental models of possible situations rather than applying formal logical rules. Errors occur when people fail to consider all possible models or represent only part of the problem.
details.whyItMatters: Mental models theory explains reasoning errors not as irrationality but as limitations in the number of mental models people can simultaneously hold and evaluate.
takeaways: People reason by building mental representations of situations
Errors arise from incomplete sets of mental models
More models means more cognitive load and more potential for error

faq.question: How does mental models theory differ from logic-based theories?
faq.answer: Logic-based theories say people apply formal rules like modus ponens. Mental models theory says people construct representations of possible scenarios and draw conclusions from them. This explains why some logically equivalent problems are much harder than others: they require more mental models.

faq.question: What predicts reasoning difficulty in this theory?
faq.answer: The number of mental models required. Problems that need only one model to solve are easy. Problems requiring two or three models are harder because people must hold multiple possibilities in working memory simultaneously. This correctly predicts which syllogisms people find difficult.
